fullText:
Summary: ACL Cables PLC (ACL.N0000), Sri Lanka's largest cable maker, is a well-run, cash-rich business: return on equity has averaged about 21% over five years and is about 18% now, it holds about Rs 10.4bn more cash and investments than debt, and it hasn't made a loss in ten years. The July–September 2026 quarter was flat: revenue rose 26% to Rs 14.30bn, but the gross margin slipped to 24% and a Rs 144mn exchange loss replaced last quarter's gain, so profit to owners was Rs 1.47bn (EPS Rs 2.04 against Rs 2.06). For the six months EPS is Rs 4.61, up 7%. Copper stock still ties up cash: inventory is Rs 19.1bn (Rs 14.1bn in March) and operating cash flow for the half was minus Rs 4.66bn, carried by selling unit trusts and Rs 4.4bn of short-term loans. A dividend of Rs 0.60 a share for 2025/26 was paid in October (Rs 0.50 a year earlier), still under 7% of profit. At Rs 101.50 (CSE close, 13 November 2026) the share trades at about 11x trailing earnings and 1.83x its NAV of Rs 55.46, against a ten-year average P/E of about 5.5x. The methods put fair value at about Rs 64.70 (Rs 63.50 before; the rise is only the higher NAV), so the price is about 57% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 55 and treat under Rs 48.50 as a strong buy.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 101.50 (CSE close, 13 November 2026). In July–September 2026 it traded between Rs 91.10 and Rs 100.50 and closed the quarter at Rs 92.00; April–June Rs 85.00–103.50; January–March Rs 81.00–107.75.
Three months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 14.30bn (up 26%), gross profit Rs 3.40bn (up 13%, margin 23.8% against 26.5%), operating profit Rs 2.57bn (up 13%), net finance income Rs 2mn (Rs 236mn) after a Rs 144mn exchange loss, profit to owners Rs 1.47bn (down 1%), EPS Rs 2.04 (Rs 2.06).
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 25.79bn (up 22%), gross margin 24.0% (28.0%), profit to owners Rs 3.31bn (up 7%), EPS Rs 4.61 (Rs 4.30). Exports Rs 6.23bn (up 46%). Net exchange gain Rs 447mn.
Twelve months to September 2026: EPS about Rs 9.13, ROE about 18%. Year to March 2026 (audited): EPS Rs 8.82, ROE about 19%.
NAV Rs 55.46 a share (September 2026). Shares in issue 718.7 million after the 1-for-3 split. The Madanayake family owns 62.1% and the EPF 10.0%.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified P/B | 37.0 | 58.2 | 90.1 | 58.2
P/E | 42.0 | 72.0 | 105.0 | 69.6
Residual income | 32.8 | 62.6 | 124.9 | 66.1
Average | 37.3 | 64.3 | 106.7 | 64.7
Fair value about Rs 64.70 (30% bear, 50% base, 20% bull), up from Rs 63.50 only because NAV rose. Buy at up to Rs 55.00 (15% below); strong buy under Rs 48.50 (25% below).

Assumptions (unchanged)
Cost of equity 18% / 16.5% / 15%, against government bonds of about 12%. Long-run ROE 14% / 17% / 20% (five-year average about 21%, including an unusually strong 2022/23 when the gross margin reached 36%). Growth 6% / 6.5% / 7%. EPS to March 2027 Rs 7.00 / 9.00 / 10.50, valued at 6 / 8 / 10 times. With Rs 4.61 earned in the first half, the base case needs Rs 4.39 in the second half, close to last year's Rs 4.52, so it still looks reasonable. Residual income starts from an ROE of 18% (19% bull).

What stands out
- Sales are growing fast (exports up 46%), but margins are thinner: 24% gross margin against 28% a year ago, as cost of sales grew faster than sales (the report doesn't say why).
- The exchange line swings: a Rs 590mn gain in April–June, a Rs 144mn loss in July–September.
- Weak cash conversion: inventory up Rs 4.95bn in six months to Rs 19.08bn; operating cash flow minus Rs 4.66bn; short-term loans up to Rs 4.43bn; net cash down to about Rs 10.4bn from Rs 14.8bn in March.
- Small payout: Rs 0.60 a share (Rs 431mn) paid October 2026, against Rs 6.3bn of profit to owners in 2025/26.

500-share plan
200 shares up to Rs 64.70, 150 up to Rs 55.00, 150 up to Rs 48.50: average about Rs 56.90, about Rs 28,465 in total. Rs 55 needs about a 46% fall from Rs 101.50, far below this year's Rs 81.00–107.75 range. Allowing for the split, the share was about Rs 41 in March 2025, so these prices are recent history, but getting back there would probably need a copper or market downturn.

What would change my view
Higher: copper staying high without hurting demand, exports growing 40%+, the gross margin recovering and stock releasing cash, a much bigger dividend, ROE above 20% without exchange gains.
Lower: a copper price fall (inventory losses, as in 2023/24), less power and construction spending, short-term loans rising further to carry stock, a stronger rupee.

Business tests: 3 of 4 passed (returns, debt, steady profit; fails on cash conversion), so it's a good business at a high price: watch list (unchanged).
